{{Short description|Example of topological space}}
In [[general topology]], the '''lexicographic ordering on the unit square''' (sometimes the '''dictionary order on the unit square'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Introduction to topological manifolds|author=Lee, John M.|date=2011|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1441979391|edition=2nd|location=New York|oclc=697506452}}</ref>) is a [[Topological space|topology]] on the [[unit square]] ''S'', i.e. on the set of points (''x'',''y'') in the [[Plane (geometry)|plane]] such that {{nowrap|1=0 ≤ ''x'' ≤ 1}} and {{nowrap|1=0 ≤ ''y'' ≤ 1.}}{{sfnp|Steen|Seebach|1995|p=73}}

== Construction ==
The [[lexicographical order]]ing gives a total ordering <math>\prec</math> on the points in the unit square: if (''x'',''y'') and (''u'',''v'') are two points in the square, {{nowrap|1=(''x'',''y'') <math>\scriptstyle\prec</math> (''u'',''v'')}} if and only if either {{nowrap|1=''x'' < ''u''}} or '''both''' {{nowrap|1=''x'' = ''u''}} '''and''' {{nowrap|1=''y'' < ''v''}}. Stated symbolically,
<math display="block">(x,y)\prec (u,v)\iff (x<u) \lor (x=u\land y<v)</math>

The lexicographic order topology on the unit square is the [[order topology]] induced by this ordering.

== Properties ==

The order topology makes ''S'' into a [[completely normal space|completely normal]] [[Hausdorff space]].{{sfnp|Steen|Seebach|1995|p=66}}  Since the lexicographical order on ''S'' can be proven to be [[Completeness (order theory)|complete]], this topology makes ''S'' into a [[compact space]].  At the same time, ''S'' contains an [[uncountable]] number of [[pairwise disjoint]] open intervals, each [[homeomorphic]] to the [[real line]], for example the intervals <math>U_x=\{(x,y):1/4<y<1/2\}</math> for <math>0\le x\le 1</math>.  So ''S'' is not [[Separable space|separable]], since any dense subset has to contain at least one point in each <math>U_x</math>.  Hence ''S'' is not [[Metrizable space|metrizable]] (since any [[compact metric space]] is separable); however, it is [[First-countable space|first countable]]. Also, S is connected and locally connected, but not path connected and not locally path connected.<ref name=":0" /> Its [[fundamental group]] is trivial.{{sfnp|Steen|Seebach|1995|p=73}}
